80129.subject: 📈 Bitcoin surges back above $86k
80129.body:
———————————————————————————

## Top Stories

**BTC** $86,502 (3.0%) | **ETH** $2,748 (1.6%) | **SOL** $122 (3.4%)

* Bitcoin reclaims [$86,000](https://x.com/WatcherGuru/status/2105876584905523415), tagging $86,912, as $110M in shorts get [wiped in 10 minutes](https://x.com/WatcherGuru/status/2105878316192354400?s=20) — US spot Bitcoin ETFs post [$148.7 million](https://cryptoslate.com/bitcoin-etfs-are-5-billion-from-a-new-flow-record-after-a-brutal-11-month-reset/) in net outflows, ending a nine-day inflow streak

* NEAR Intents freezes cross-chain swaps after a bug [drains about $3.8M](https://x.com/DecryptMedia/status/2105960988990218372) and says it will repay users — NEAR GM [identifies the attacker](https://x.com/TheBlockCo/status/2105960701139263553) and gives them 48 hours to return the funds

* US Treasury yields hit a [24-year high](https://x.com/qz/status/2105870616154788325) as the 10-year touches 5.34%

* Broadcom agrees to lend Anthropic up to [$42 billion](https://x.com/DeItaone/status/2105598829114585494) for AI infrastructure leases

* Citigroup raises its 12-month Bitcoin price forecast to [$113,000](https://x.com/wallstengine/status/2105588647181553983) from $82,000

* SEC proposes a new [custody framework](https://x.com/TheBlockCo/status/2105750569851953576) for crypto assets held by investment advisers

* Pump Fun leads onchain protocols with[ $2.6m of revenue](https://x.com/Tyler_Did_It/status/2105981117568303434?s=20)

* September crypto hack losses exceed [$766 million](https://x.com/Saanjana_Nikita/status/2105569313902215650), the worst month of 2026 so far — Bitget's $388M hack pushes Q3 crypto security losses to [$1.26 billion](https://cointelegraph.com/news/bitget-hack-q3-industry-losses-1-26-billion)

* AI-native cybersecurity company Armadin raises a [$255.5 million](https://x.com/pulse2news/status/2105607332642345313) Series B led by a16z and Accel, valued over $2.5 billion

* MetaMask security incident forces roughly [523,000 ETH](https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2026/10/01/metamask-security-incident-forces-ethereum-staking-exits-with-lido-warning-of-lost-rewards) to unstake

* Bank of England warns AI valuations are vulnerable to a [deeper selloff](https://x.com/DeItaone/status/2105237257896546770) than July's

* Amazon plans to sell [$8 billion](https://x.com/WhaleInsider/status/2105881086442221921) of Nvidia chips to investors

* Volantis raises [$88 million](https://x.com/AGTPinsights/status/2105650884894130612) to build optical links connecting AI chips to memory

* Brazil's CSD BR partners with Ripple to mirror securities records on the [XRP Ledger](https://x.com/Cointelegraph/status/2105119223030685888)

* TokenWorks opens backing for [BitMON by Des Lucréce](https://x.com/token_works/status/2105689204881592631)

80125.subject: What is this century’s biggest idea?
80125.body:
The Economist Picks

Автор: The Economist


Автор: The Economist

    
    
    Прочитайте цю статтю на LinkedIn, щоб приєднатися до обговорення
Прочитати на LinkedIn
https://www.linkedin.com/comm/pulse/what-centurys-biggest-idea-the-economist-eqsge?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_series_follow_newsletter_02%3Ba8caMkiRQSOTrMueUs5SuQ%3D%3D&midToken=AQFTjFOONAfT2w&midSig=23tGcjA_-Ltss1&trk=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_&trkEmail=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_-null-fz96fz~muqvbsys~mx-null-null&eid=fz96fz-muqvbsys-mx
  
Enjoying this newsletter? Get it in your inbox every Thursday, as well as our bonus weekend round-up of The Economist’s best journalism, by signing up for free here. When I was a student I sold Christmas cards to raise money for UNICEF. To potential donors sipping ale in English pubs, I’d stress that for less than the price of a pint they could pay for a vaccine shot that might save the life of a child in Africa. Many reached for their wallets, but I remember one who said, in a rather peeved voice: “Why don’t you raise money for British children?” It is a fair question. I was taking a hyper-rational approach to charity: the same donation can relieve far more suffering in a poor country than in a rich one. But many people feel more empathy for those closer by. In “Bleak House” Charles Dickens mocked a character called Mrs Jellyby, who was obsessed with helping the inhabitants of Borrioboola-Gha, a fictional sub-Saharan locale, while neglecting her own home and children. I wonder what Dickens—let alone the man in that pub—would have made of the “effective altruists” (EAs) who now dominate Silicon Valley. As we report this week, their philosophy is the biggest idea of this century so far. And it takes the Mrs Jellyby principle to extremes. Not only do far-away people have the same claim on our goodwill as those standing next to us. Many EAs think we should care—a lot—about the billions or trillions of people who may be born in the distant future. Some also think that, because animals can suffer, we should worry as much about prawns as we do about people. Our cover package explores these ideas. Only a few people are EAs, but they are hugely influential, since they staff the most advanced artificial-intelligence companies. Some of their insights are sound. It really is better if charity is cost-effective, and we really should take seriously the possibility that AI could go rogue and do immense harm. But sometimes their logic leads them to odd places. If your moral calculations depend on predicting what the world will be like in the year 2300, there is a good chance they will be hooey. And if you are both powerful and utterly convinced you know what’s best for humanity—well, that combination didn’t work out so well during some of the high-minded revolutions of the past, from France’s in 1789 to Russia’s in 1917.
